passages.text: What then? Do not even the celebrated wise men prefer pleasure, and did they not have relations with whichever women they wished? First among them is the teacher of Greece, about whom Phoebus himself said, ‘Of all men, Socrates is wisest.’ Does he not propose that women be held in common in the best-governed city, Lacedaemon, and cover the handsome Alcibiades beneath his cloak? The Socratic Antisthenes also writes that one should not reject so-called adultery. And does not his pupil Diogenes openly have relations with Lais, in return for carrying her publicly on his shoulders? Does not Epicurus prefer pleasure? Does not Aristippus, after being perfumed, give his whole self to Aphrodite? Does not Zeno, hinting at treating things as indifferent, say that the divine is present through everything, so that intelligent people may recognize that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself, and that forbidding so-called adulteries or unions with a mother, daughter, sister, or children is superfluous? Chrysippus, in his love letters, also mentions the image in Argos, placing Hera's face at Zeus's genitals.

lexical_decisions.chosen: propose that women be held in common
lexical_decisions.rationale: The claim is assigned to Socrates in the source and retained as the letter writer's claim. It is not silently reassigned to another philosopher or rewritten into a historically corrected account.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ μισθῷ τοῦ φέρειν αὐτὴν ἐπ’ ὤμων δημοσίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: in return for carrying her publicly on his shoulders
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive specifies the payment or recompense as carrying Lais. The rendering does not add money, identify a fee amount, or reverse who carries whom.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hinting at treating things as indifferent
lexical_decisions.rationale: Indifference is the philosophical treatment of the acts as morally neither good nor bad, not simply emotional unconcern. The source presents this as an indirect implication, retained as hinting rather than an explicit quotation from Zeno.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μίξεις μητρὸς ἢ θυγατρὸς ἢ ἀδελφῆς ἢ παίδων
lexical_decisions.chosen: unions with a mother, daughter, sister, or children
lexical_decisions.rationale: Children preserves the broad age and relationship range of παῖδες. Boys is possible in this sexual context, but the adjacent family categories also support children; the source does not name particular ages.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τῷ τοῦ Διὸς αἰδοίῳ φέρων τῆς Ἥρας τὸ πρόσωπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: placing Hera's face at Zeus's genitals
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle concerns the writer's description of the image. The precise position is retained without adding an act not expressly named in the supplied wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ Ἀρίστιππος μυρισθεὶς ὅλον αὐτὸν Ἀφροδίτῃ χαρίζεται;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Does not Aristippus, after being perfumed, give his whole self to Aphrodite?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes whole self with the finite giving verb, foregrounding his complete self-dedication to Aphrodite after perfuming. The alternative Does not Aristippus, perfumed all over, give himself to Aphrodite takes whole self as an accusative of respect with perfumed and foregrounds the extent of perfuming. Both attachments are viable; the chosen one keeps the full accusative expression as what is given rather than leaving the giving object to inference alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα γνώριμον τοῖς συνετοῖς γένηται ἵνα ᾧ ἂν τις μιγῇ, ὡς ἑαυτῷ μίγνυται
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that intelligent people may recognize that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied wording repeats ἵνα. The first clause is purposive; the main text reads the second clause loosely as the content of the intended recognition, which the phrase become known calls for in this context. A material alternative preserves the repeated purpose force, so that it may become known to the intelligent ... so that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself. Their exact syntactic relationship remains uncertain. No substitution of an unprinted ὅτι or other Greek emendation has been supplied.

passages.text: I know that these things appear terrifying and utterly shameful to those uninitiated in the truth, but not to the gods and philosophers of the Greeks, nor to the mysteries of Dionysus and Demeter. But, after all this, so that I do not waste time recounting the lives of every god and philosopher, let two be your greatest models: Zeus among gods, and Socrates among human philosophers. Having understood the rest from what I have reminded you of in writing, take care never to distress a lover of yours. For if you act against gods and lovers, you will be judged impious and undergo the appropriate punishment. But if you offer yourself to every lover, then, as an imitator of the gods, you will obtain their beneficence. For the rest, dearest, remember the mysteries I have disclosed to you and show me your decision in writing. Farewell.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The initiation image is explicit and continues into the reference to mysteries. Uninformed would be smoother but would erase the writer's claim to privileged initiatory knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let two be your greatest models
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can mean marks, aims, or objects of attention. The two exemplary figures and the subsequent imitation argument favor models; the rendering does not make them legal authorities or assign a new office.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν δὲ παντὶ ἐραστῇ ἑαυτὴν παράσχῃς
lexical_decisions.chosen: if you offer yourself to every lover
lexical_decisions.rationale: The universal every and reflexive yourself are retained as the letter writer's demand. The translation reports his coercive argument without adopting it or adding detail.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ ἐξ ὧν σοι γράψας ὑπέμνησα συνεῖσα ἔπεχε, μήποτε ἐραστήν σου λυπήσῃς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Having understood the rest from what I have reminded you of in writing, take care never to distress a lover of yours
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the rest as the object of understanding and the written reminders as its basis, explicitly preserving ἐξ as from. An alternative treats the rest adverbially, for the rest, while still requiring an understanding drawn from those reminders. The prior wording made the reminders themselves the direct object and has been corrected.

passages.text: They were not gods, then, but veiled representations of tyrants. For a tomb of Cronus is shown in the Caucasian mountains—not in heaven but on earth—the tomb of a savage man who devoured his children. A tomb of the sexually unrestrained Zeus of myth, who likewise swallowed his daughter Metis, is also seen in Crete. There is also Pluto's tomb at the Acherusian lake, Poseidon's on Tenos, the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae, Hermes' at Hermopolis, Ares' in Thrace, Aphrodite's on Cyprus, Dionysus' at Thebes, and those of others in other places. In any case, the tombs of the very gods mentioned are visible. For they were humans, and wicked ones and sorcerers at that. They could not otherwise have become absolute rulers—I mean the Zeus of myth and Dionysus—unless, through transformation into whatever they themselves wished, they held sway over whomever they wished.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes enigmatic or figurative representations. The claim identifies the mythic gods as disguised presentations of human tyrants, not merely difficult riddles that tyrants posed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἡλίου δὲ ἐν Ἄτροις καὶ Σελήνης ἐν Κάρραις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae
lexical_decisions.rationale: The divine names are rendered by their transparent celestial meanings; Helios and Selene are conventional name alternatives. Atroi follows the supplied place-name spelling without silently identifying it with another city.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μὴ τῇ μεταμορφώσει ὧν ἤθελον ἐπεκράτουν εἰς ὅπερ αὐτοὶ ἤθελον
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless, through transformation into whatever they themselves wished, they held sway over whomever they wished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches into whatever they themselves wished to transformation, retaining the explicit changing-form image that matches the preceding accounts of assumed forms. The material alternative unless through transformation they gained control over whomever they wished for whatever purpose they themselves wished takes the final phrase as the intended end of domination. The source does not expressly settle whose form changes, so no otherwise unnamed magical mechanism is supplied.

passages.text: If we must emulate their lives, let us imitate not only their adulteries but also their tables. For Cronus swallowed his own children, and Zeus likewise his own daughter. And what need is there to say more? Pelops became a dinner for all the gods. So let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a dinner like the gods'. Then the dinner would be worthy of the marriages. But you would never bear to do this, just as I would never bear to commit adultery. Besides all this, you threaten me with the wrath of Love as though he were a powerful god. Love is not a god such as he is thought to be, but a desire arising from the constitution of the living being for the succession of life, according to the providence of the one who brought everything into being. This is so that the whole race may never fail, but, on the pretext of pleasure, another may again come into being from the substance of the one who is going to die, sprung from a lawful marriage, so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age. Those born from adultery would not be able to do this, lacking a natural affection toward those who begot them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And what need is there to say more?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rhetorical question concerns what needs saying, not what one is able to say. More is supplied from the movement toward the final example, rather than changing the question into an appeal to ability.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from the constitution of the living being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun refers to the mixture or constitution of the organism. Animal is another literal rendering of ζῷον, but living being preserves its applicability to humans in this explanation.

The same pretext language used in the polemic is retained in the positive account of generation. For the sake of pleasure would flatten the distinction between the reproductive purpose and the pleasure that provides its occasion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως πρὸς τὸ γηροτροφεῖν τὸν αὐτοῦ πατέρα γνώσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age
lexical_decisions.rationale: The child is the inferred subject of knowing, with the father its expressed object and support in old age the purpose. The source's ensuing assertion about children born from adultery is retained as the fictional letter writer's claim, not presented as an established psychological fact.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν καὶ ἡμεῖς πρὸ τῶν ἀθεμίτων γάμων ὅμοιον δεῖπνον τοῖς θεοῖς ἐπιτελέσωμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: So let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a dinner like the gods'
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative gods is read comparatively because the preceding instruction explicitly calls for imitation of the gods' tables. A material alternative reads it as beneficiaries: let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a similar dinner for the gods. That alternative would propose a banquet offered to them rather than only a banquet modeled on theirs; the main text does not claim to exclude it grammatically.
